introduction: Why was the world made, and each of us in it? These readings answer many times over, mostly in Bahá’u’lláh's own short sentences: creation is for love; human beings were created to know God and to worship him; since God is known through his Manifestation, all were created to recognize him in his Day; and the Manifestations come for the reformation of the world and the refinement of souls. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that a creation ending in the material life alone would be in vain, a tree without fruit. A hundred of the guide's hundred and eleven quotations are read here beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the Qur'an's 'I created jinn and humankind only that they might worship me', the Westminster catechism's 'chief end of man', Isaiah's 'for my glory', Augustine's restless heart, 'this is life eternal, that they might know thee', Micah's summary, Paul at Athens. Nine push back or add a side: Khayyam, who came 'why not knowing'; Spinoza, for whom final causes are human figments; Macbeth; Hardy; the Preacher's 'time and chance'; Nietzsche's rope over an abyss; Paine on revelation as hearsay; the Qur'an's 'that ye may know one another'; and Candide's garden.
questions: The readings give several purposes: love, knowledge, worship, recognition, the betterment of the world. Are these one purpose or several?
'He created you only for your own selves.' What does God gain from being known and worshipped, according to the readings and to Job's friend Elihu?
Spinoza called final causes human figments; Khayyam did not know why he came. What would you say to each?
If the purpose of creation is recognition of the Manifestation, what of those who lived and died without hearing of him?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says a life for the body alone would make creation 'in vain'. Candide tends his garden. Is that vain?
How would you tell whether you were living for the purpose these readings describe?

outside.why: Dante ends his poem with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
The Wisdom of Solomon says to God: never wouldest thou have made any thing, if thou hadst hated it.
Paul is confident that all things work together for good to them that love God.
Genesis says: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
Isaiah says of the earth that God created it not in vain; he formed it to be inhabited.
The Qur'an asks: deemed ye then that We had created you for naught?
The Westminster catechism opens with the same answer: man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.
Julian of Norwich asked the meaning of what she was shown, and was told: love was his meaning.
John's Gospel says: this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God.
A psalm says: thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing.
Khayyam found himself come into this universe 'and why not knowing', and going out 'I know not whither'. What would count as knowing the purpose?
The elders in the Apocalypse say: thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.
Elihu asks Job: if thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand?
The Qur'an says: I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship me.
The Preacher's conclusion: fear God, and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
Proverbs says that the Lord hath made all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil.
Spinoza wrote that nature has no particular goal in view, and that final causes are mere human figments. Is 'purpose' something found in creation, or brought to it?
A psalm says: the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Isaiah has God say of each one called by his name: I have created him for my glory.
Augustine says to God: you have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.
Proverbs says that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
Paul told the Athenians that God made all nations that they should seek the Lord, and feel after him, and find him.
Jeremiah says: let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.
Paul says the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
Hosea hears God say of his own people: my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.
The Qur'an says: We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves.
Job says at the end: I had heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee.
Paul says: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
The Qur'an gives another purpose: We made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Is knowing God reached apart from knowing people?
A psalmist desires one thing: to behold the beauty of the Lord.
Macbeth finds that life is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. What does a purpose have to be for a person to live by it?
Deuteronomy asks what the Lord requires: to fear him, to walk in his ways, to love and to serve him, for thy good.
Jesus said: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no man cometh unto the Father but by me.
Paul says that all things were created by him, and for him.
Micah asks what the Lord requires: to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
A psalm says: thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
Ephesians says: we are his workmanship, created unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Proverbs says: the hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the Lord hath made even both of them.
Jesus said of some: seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not.
A psalmist says: when thou saidst, seek ye my face, my heart said, thy face, Lord, will I seek.
The Qur'an says that in the remembrance of God hearts find rest.
Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
Jesus said: make the tree good and his fruit good, for the tree is known by his fruit.
Paul says that when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son.
Peter said: in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.
Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent, and revealing them unto babes.
A psalm asks, as the hart pants for water: when shall I come and appear before God?
John's Gospel says that all things were made by the Word, and without him was not any thing made.
Jesus said: seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
Jesus told Philip: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
John says the world was made by him, and the world knew him not.
Paine held that a revelation is revelation to the first person only, and hearsay to every other. Can the purpose of every life be the recognition of one person?
Simeon had waited all his life, and said: now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, for mine eyes have seen.
A psalm says: this is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
Mordecai asked Esther: who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
Jesus said that many prophets desired to see the things his disciples saw.
Paul wrote that now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
Joel foresees a day when the spirit is poured out on all flesh.
Jesus said that the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.
Paul says: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling.
Jesus said: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?
A psalmist asks: what shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me?
Jesus said that Mary had chosen the good part, which shall not be taken away.
Jesus ended a parable of invited guests with the words: many are called, but few are chosen.
The merchant in the parable sold all he had for one pearl of great price.
Isaiah says: the ox knoweth his owner, but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider.
Plato pictures prisoners who see only shadows and take them for the whole.
Ecclesiastes saw that the race is not to the swift, but time and chance happeneth to them all. If life has an appointed purpose, why does it look like this?
Paul asks: shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, why hast thou made me thus?
Jesus said: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
Paul compares the law to tutors and governors set over an heir until the time appointed.
Nietzsche called man a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman, a rope over an abyss. Is a purpose given to us, or made by us?
Paul says: if in this life only we have hope, we are of all men most miserable.
The Preacher asks what profit a man has of all his labour under the sun, and answers: vanity.
Aristotle held that the final cause moves all things as being loved.
Hardy asked why joy lies slain and hope unblooms, and found only crass casualty and dicing time. What shows that things exist for a purpose?
Whitman says that for him the nebula cohered to an orb and the long slow strata piled.
A psalm says: O Lord, how manifold are thy works; the earth is full of thy riches.
The rich man in the parable told his soul: take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
A psalm says that man in honour who understands not is like the beasts that perish.
Aristotle held that the life according to reason is best for man, since reason more than anything else is man.
Jesus said: that which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Ezekiel hears the promise: a new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.
Isaiah calls: ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters.
Malachi promises that unto those who fear his name the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing.
John's first letter says that he that loveth not knoweth not God, for God is love.
Longfellow wrote that our destined end is to act, that each tomorrow find us farther than today.
James says: count it all joy when ye fall into trials, for the trying of your faith worketh patience.
Paul says: we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.
Voltaire's Candide, after every theory has failed him, concludes that we must take care of our garden. Is looking to 'the end' the only wisdom?
Tennyson looked to one far-off divine event to which the whole creation moves.
Micah foresees every man under his vine and fig tree, and none to make them afraid.
Jesus read: he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives.
Isaiah foresees nations beating their swords into plowshares, and learning war no more.
Jesus said: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.
Proverbs says that righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
Paul noticed that not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble, were called.
The Qur'an says: let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly.
The Qur'an says to its Prophet: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.
A psalm says: how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
